Name the three particles inside an atom.
protons, neutrons and electrons
Is water an element or a compound?
How do you know?
A compound.
It has two types of atom, H and O, joined together.
element: a substance made of only one type of atom
Every element has its own box on the periodic table.
Which number in the box tells you which element it is?
The atomic number.
It counts the protons.

Q1
Oxygen gas is made of O₂ particles: two O atoms bonded together. So oxygen is
Aan element
Ba compound
Ca mixture
Dan ion
An element.
Both atoms are O: only one type of atom.
Two atoms per particle makes it diatomic.
Q2
Monatomic?
An element made of single atoms. e.g. He, Ne
Diatomic?
An element made of two atoms of the same type bonded together. e.g. O₂, Cl₂
Compound?
Two or more types of atom bonded in a fixed ratio. e.g. H₂O
Q3
Which particle adds almost nothing to the mass of an atom?
Athe proton
Bthe neutron
Cthe electron
Dthey are all the same
The electron: 0.0005 amu,
or $9.109 \times 10^{-28}$ g.
About $\frac{1}{1840}$ of a proton.
Q4
Proton?
Positive. In the nucleus. 1 amu ($1.673 \times 10^{-24}$ g).
Neutron?
No charge. In the nucleus. 1 amu ($1.675 \times 10^{-24}$ g).
Electron?
Negative. In shells. 0.0005 amu ($9.109 \times 10^{-28}$ g).

Q5
Magnesium is written ${}^{24}_{12}\mathrm{Mg}$. What does the 24 count?
Aprotons
Bneutrons
Cprotons + neutrons
Delectrons
The mass number: protons + neutrons.
The 12 is the atomic number: the protons.
Cambridge 1A Skills: the number of neutronsHow many neutrons are in ${}^{24}_{12}\mathrm{Mg}$?
1Mass number
top number $= 24$   (protons + neutrons)
2Atomic number
bottom number $= 12$   (protons)
3Subtract
neutrons $=$ mass number $-$ atomic number $= 24 - 12$
4Answer
neutrons $=$ $12$
${}^{24}_{12}\mathrm{Mg}$ has 12 neutrons.
Cambridge 1A Skills: the number of electrons in an ionHow many electrons are in the phosphide ion, ${}^{31}_{15}\mathrm{P}^{3-}$?
1Protons
atomic number $= 15$, so $15$ protons
2Neutral atom
a neutral P atom has $15$ electrons
3Read the charge
$3-$ means it has gained 3 electrons
4Electrons
$15 + 3 =$ $18$
The phosphide ion has 18 electrons. The protons never change.
Q6
How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in ${}^{65}_{30}\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$?
patomic number: $30$ protons
n$65 - 30 = 35$ neutrons
e$2+$ means it lost 2: $30 - 2 = 28$ electrons
Write the atomic notation for a particle with 11 protons, 12 neutrons and 10 electrons.
${}^{23}_{11}\mathrm{Na}^{+}$   (mass number $11 + 12 = 23$; one electron fewer: $1+$)
How many neutrons are in ${}^{37}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}$?
$37 - 17 = 20$ neutrons
How many electrons are in ${}^{27}_{13}\mathrm{Al}^{3+}$?
$13 - 3 = 10$ electrons

Q1
Nitrogen-14 and nitrogen-15 are both nitrogen. What is different about their atoms?
Athe protons
Bthe neutrons
Cthe electrons
Dnothing at all
The neutrons: 7 and 8.
Both have 7 protons, so both are nitrogen. They are isotopes.
Q2
Do isotopes of an element have a different atomic number or a different mass number?
A different mass number.
Same protons (same atomic number), different neutrons.

9 protons, 10 neutrons, 9 electrons
${}^{35}_{17}\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$
17 protons, 18 neutrons, 18 electrons (gained 1)

19 protons: fluorine, atomic number 9

Q5
Chlorine atoms have mass numbers of 35 or 37. The periodic table gives chlorine 35.5, not 36. Why?
Aevery Cl atom has mass 35.5
Bmost Cl atoms are chlorine-35
CCl has half a neutron
Dit is rounded wrongly
It is an average, weighted by how common each isotope is.
About 3 in 4 atoms are chlorine-35.

Why is the relative atomic mass on the periodic table not a whole number?
It is the average mass of the atoms,
weighted by the abundance of each isotope.

Atomthe smallest piece of an element that retains the properties of that element
Subatomic particlea particle that is present within an atom; includes protons, neutrons and electrons
Protona positively charged subatomic particle present within the nucleus of an atom
Neutronan uncharged subatomic particle present within the nucleus of an atom
Electrona negatively charged subatomic particle that moves around the nucleus of an atom
Elementa pure substance made of only one type of atom
Compounda substance formed from two or more different types of atoms in a fixed ratio
Monatomican element that consists of only one atom
Diatomican element that consists of two atoms
Physical propertythe features of a substance that can be measured without altering its chemical composition
Chemical propertythe behaviour of a substance when it reacts with another substance
Atomic numberthe number of protons present in the nucleus of an atom
Mass numberthe total number of protons and neutrons present in the nucleus of an atom
Isotopean atom of the same element with the same number of protons but a different number of neutrons (different mass number)
Iona positively or negatively charged atom that has either lost or gained electron(s)
Relative atomic massthe average of the relative masses of all atoms of an element, based on its isotopes and their natural percentage abundances
${}^{39}_{19}\mathrm{K}^{+}$: how many protons, neutrons and electrons? Atom, ion or isotope?
19 protons, 20 neutrons, 18 electrons. An ion: it has lost one electron.
Elements and compounds
Atom: smallest piece of an element.
Element: only ONE type of atom.
Compound: 2 or more types of atom,
bonded in a fixed ratio.
e.g. H₂O: always 2 H to 1 O
Giant structures can be elements
(C, Cu) or compounds (NaCl).
Count the types of atom!
Subatomic particles
proton p⁺: positive, nucleus
1 amu = 1.673 × 10⁻²⁴ g
neutron n: no charge, nucleus
1 amu = 1.675 × 10⁻²⁴ g
electron e⁻: negative, shells
0.0005 amu = 9.109 × 10⁻²⁸ g
Atomic notation
${}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X}^{\text{charge}}$${}^{24}_{12}\mathrm{Mg}$
$Z$ = atomic number = protons
(sets the element)
$A$ = mass number = protons + neutrons
neutrons = $A - Z$
neutral atom: electrons = protons
Cambridge 1A Skills
Neutrons in ${}^{24}_{12}\mathrm{Mg}$?
1$A = 24$, $Z = 12$
2neutrons $= 24 - 12 = 12$
Electrons in ${}^{31}_{15}\mathrm{P}^{3-}$?
115 protons, so neutral P has 15 e⁻
2$3-$: gained 3 electrons
3electrons $= 15 + 3 = 18$
The phosphide ion has 18 electrons.
Isotopes and ions
Isotopes: same element (same protons),
different neutrons, so different $A$.
e.g. ${}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N}$ and ${}^{15}_{7}\mathrm{N}$
Ion: an atom that has lost or gained e⁻.
lost e⁻: positive ion. e.g. Mg²⁺
gained e⁻: negative ion. e.g. F⁻
positive ion $\mathrm{M}^{x+}$: e⁻ $= Z - x$
negative ion $\mathrm{X}^{y-}$: e⁻ $= Z + y$
Relative atomic mass
The decimal on the periodic table.
Average mass of the atoms, weighted
by how common each isotope is.
e.g. Cl = 35.5: mostly chlorine-35
! Ions change electrons, never protons.
! 35.5 is the relative atomic mass,
not a mass number.
You try
How many protons, neutrons and
electrons are in ${}^{32}_{16}\mathrm{S}^{2-}$?
p$Z = 16$: 16 protons
n$32 - 16 = 16$ neutrons
e$2-$: gained 2, $16 + 2 = 18$ electrons
16 p, 16 n, 18 e⁻ (a sulfide ion)
How many electrons does a neutral oxygen atom have? How do you know?
8.
Atomic number 8, so 8 protons, and a neutral atom has as many electrons as protons.
Sodium forms the ion Na⁺.
What happened to the sodium atom?
It lost one electron.
11 protons, 10 electrons.
A sodium compound is held in a flame.
The flame turns bright yellow. Where could the light come from?
From the electrons in the sodium atoms.
(We find out how in this lesson.)
a flame test: heating a substance and looking at the colour

Q1
Hydrogen gas glows when a current passes through it. Through a prism you see only a few sharp coloured lines, not a full rainbow. Why?
Athe prism is too small
Belectrons can only have certain energies
Cthe nucleus gives out light
Dhydrogen burns
Electrons sit in shells with fixed energies.
Each fall between two shells gives out one exact energy: one colour.
Q2
Ground state or excited state: which one gives out light?
The excited state, as the electron falls back down to a lower shell.
Why does every element have its own emission spectrum?
Its shells have their own energies, so the falls give their own colours.
Q3
A shell can hold at most $2n^2$ electrons, where $n$ is the shell number. How many can shell 3 hold?
A8
B9
C18
D32
$2 \times 3^2 = 18$.
But the outer shell never holds more than 8. Shell 3 stops at 8 until shell 4 has 2.
Cambridge Worked example 1B–1Using the Bohr model, write the electron configuration for oxygen.
1Atomic number
oxygen $= 8$, so 8 electrons
2Period
row 2, so 2 shells
3Shell 1
holds $2(1)^2 = 2$ electrons
4Shell 2
the rest: $8 - 2 = 6$
5Write it
2,6
Oxygen is 2,6. It has 6 valence electrons.
Cambridge Worked example 1B–3Determine the electron configuration for an oxide ion, O²⁻.
1The atom
oxygen atom: 8 electrons, 2,6
2Read the charge
$2-$ means it gained 2 electrons: $8 + 2 = 10$
3Refill the shells
2 in shell 1, the other 8 in shell 2
4Write it
2,8
O²⁻ is 2,8: a full outer shell, the same as neon.
Q4
Write the electron configuration for each.
He2
N2,5
Ca2,8,8,2
Zn2,8,18,2  (30 electrons: shell 3 fills to 18 after shell 4 has 2)
Q5
Draw the Bohr model for lithium and for chlorine.
Li 2,1   Cl 2,8,7
Q6
How many valence electrons (in the outer shell)?
Al2,8,3: 3
S2,8,6: 6
Li⁺lost 1, so 2: 2 (shell 1 is now the outer shell)
Br⁻gained 1: 8

Q7
The Bohr model could not explain the spectra of atoms with many electrons. A newer model splits shells into smaller parts. How many electrons can the smallest part, an orbital, hold?
A1
B2
C8
D$2n^2$
2.
Shells hold subshells. Subshells hold orbitals. Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons.
ShellSubshellsOrbitals in eachElectrons in eachShell total
1s122
2s, p1, 32, 68
3s, p, d1, 3, 52, 6, 1018
4s, p, d, f1, 3, 5, 72, 6, 10, 1432

Every orbital holds 2 electrons, so each subshell holds 2 × its orbitals. The shell totals match $2n^2$.

Q8
Shell, subshell, orbital: what is each one?
Shell: an energy level. Subshell (s, p, d, f): part of a shell. Orbital: a region in a subshell that holds up to 2 electrons.
How many orbitals in s, p and d?
s: 1   p: 3   d: 5
Q9
State one limitation of the Bohr model of the atom.
It cannot explain the complex emission spectra of atoms with many electrons.
It treats electrons as particles in fixed shells, with no subshells or orbitals.
Why is potassium 2,8,8,1 and not 2,8,9?
The outer shell holds no more than 8. Shell 4 starts before shell 3 fills to 18.
Write the Bohr configuration of calcium.
2,8,8,2
How many orbitals are in a p subshell? How many electrons can it hold?
3 orbitals, 6 electrons
Today we work on the ones not ticked yet.
Q1
Aufbau's principle?
Electrons fill the lowest energy subshells first.
Hund's rule?
In a subshell, each orbital gets one electron before any orbital gets a second.
Which fills first, 4s or 3d?
4s. It is slightly lower in energy.
Worked example (after Cambridge 1B Skills)Use the periodic table to write the subshell configuration for sulfur.
1Find it
S: atomic number 16, period 3, group 16
2Block
groups 13 to 18 are the p block
3Last subshell
4th along the p block in period 3: 3p⁴
4Fill below it
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴
5Check
$2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 4 = 16$ electrons ✓
Sulfur: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴, or [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴

Q4
Why does the sodium ion, Na⁺, have the same electron configuration as neon?
Na (2,8,1) loses its 1 valence electron.
That leaves 10 electrons, 2,8 or 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, exactly like neon.
Write the subshell configuration of K⁺.
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶  (19 − 1 = 18 electrons)
Write the subshell configuration of potassium.
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹
An electron falls from shell 3 to shell 2. Is energy absorbed or released?
Released, as light of one exact energy (one colour).

Bohr modelalso called the shell model. Shows the position of electrons in shells around the nucleus
Emission spectrumthe electromagnetic radiation emitted by a source, such as atoms
Excited statewhen electron(s) in an atom have gained energy and are no longer in their lowest possible energy state
Ground statewhen all electrons in an atom are in their lowest possible energy state, closest to the nucleus
Valence shellthe outermost shell of an atom
Valence electronan electron found in the outermost shell of an atom
Subshella region within a shell made of a certain number of orbitals. Subshells are labelled s, p, d and f
Orbitala three-dimensional description of the most likely location of an electron in an atom. Each holds zero, one or two electrons
Aufbau's principledescribes the order of filling subshells with electrons, from their lowest possible energy levels first
Hund's ruleevery orbital in a subshell contains one electron before any orbital is fully occupied with two electrons
Why does each metal give its own flame colour?
Its electron shells have their own energies, so the energy released as excited electrons fall back is different for each metal.
The Bohr (shell) model
Electrons sit in shells around the nucleus.
Ground state: all e⁻ in the lowest shells.
Excited state: e⁻ gains energy, jumps up.
Falling back gives out light of one
exact energy: one colour.
Emission spectrum: lines unique to
each element, like a fingerprint.
Filling the shells
max in shell $n$ $= 2n^2$2, 8, 18, 32
Lowest (closest) shells fill first.
Outer shell holds no more than 8.
e.g. K is 2,8,8,1 not 2,8,9
Valence shell: the outer shell.
Valence electrons: e⁻ in it.
Shells, subshells, orbitals
shell → subshells (s, p, d, f) → orbitals
each orbital holds max 2 e⁻
s: 1 orbital, 2 e⁻   p: 3 orbitals, 6 e⁻
d: 5 orbitals, 10 e⁻   f: 7 orbitals, 14 e⁻
Bohr's limit: cannot explain spectra
of atoms with many electrons.
Cambridge WE 1B–1 and 1B–3

1$Z = 8$: 8 electrons, period 2
2shell 1: 2   shell 2: $8 - 2 = 6$
3O is 2,6
Oxide ion, O²⁻?
1$2-$: gained 2, so $8 + 2 = 10$ e⁻
2O²⁻ is 2,8 (like neon)
Subshell notation
1s² 2s² 2p²carbon
number = shell, letter = subshell,
superscript = electrons in it
Aufbau: lowest energy fills first:
1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p
Hund's rule: one e⁻ per orbital
before any orbital gets a second.
Exceptions: Cr [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵
Cu [Ar] 4s¹ 3d¹⁰
Shorthand: Al 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹
= [Ne] 3s² 3p¹
! 4s fills before 3d.
! Superscripts add to the number
of electrons. Always check.
Worked example: sulfur
1S: $Z = 16$, period 3, group 16
2p block, 4th along: ends 3p⁴
31s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴
4check: $2+2+6+2+4 = 16$ ✓
Worked example: Al³⁺
1Al: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹
2$3+$: lost 3 valence e⁻ (3s² 3p¹)
3Al³⁺: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ (like neon)

Q1
Lithium, sodium and potassium all react strongly with water. What do their atoms have in common?
Athe same number of shells
Bthe same number of valence electrons
Cthe same mass
Dthe same number of protons
One valence electron each: they are all in group 1.
Same group, similar outer shell, similar chemistry.
Q2
What is the difference between a group and a period?
A group is a column (18 of them). A period is a row (7 of them).
What do elements in the same group share? In the same period?
Group: the same number of valence electrons, so similar properties.
Period: the same number of occupied shells.
Q3
Chlorine (2,8,7) has 17 protons. How much positive charge does one of its valence electrons really feel pulling on it?
A+17
B+7
C+1
Dnone
About +7.
The 10 inner-shell electrons cancel 10 of the 17 protons.
Cambridge Worked example 1C–1Determine the core charge of a magnesium atom.
1Protons
atomic number $= 12$
2Configuration
2,8,2
3Inner shells
all but the valence shell: $2 + 8 = 10$
4Subtract
core charge $= 12 - 10 =$ $+2$
Magnesium has a core charge of +2. Core charge is always positive.
Q4
Fluorine
2,7:  $9 - 2 = +7$
Potassium
2,8,8,1:  $19 - 18 = +1$
So which nucleus pulls its valence electron harder?
Fluorine: a bigger core charge, and its valence shell is only shell 2.
Q5
Why does core charge stay the same down a group, but rise across a period?
Down a group: one more proton for every extra inner electron.
Across a period: one more proton each time, but no new inner shell.

N: 2,5, so $7 - 2 = +5$. Rb: $37 - 36 = +1$.
Nitrogen: a bigger core charge, and only two shells.

Q1
Sodium and chlorine are both in period 3. Which atom is bigger?
Asodium
Bchlorine, it has more electrons
Cthey are the same size
Dit depends on the isotope
Sodium (190 pm against 79 pm).
Same three shells, but chlorine's core charge (+7) pulls them in much harder than sodium's (+1).
Cambridge Worked example 1C–4Which element's atom has the larger atomic radius, lithium or potassium? Explain.
1Define
Atomic radius is the distance from the centre of the nucleus to the valence shell.
2Key difference
Both are in group 1, so both have a core charge of +1. Li is in period 2, K is in period 4.
3Relate back
K has more shells (4) than Li (2), so potassium has the larger atomic radius.
Q2
Further right in the same period means a greater core charge.
True. One more proton each step, no new inner shell.
Higher up a group means a larger atomic radius.
False. Higher up means fewer shells, so a smaller radius.
Q3
Which atom has the larger atomic radius, carbon or oxygen? Explain.
1Atomic radius: centre of the nucleus to the valence shell.
2Both in period 2. Core charge: C +4, O +6.
3C's smaller core charge pulls its valence electrons less, so carbon is larger.

Back in your seat when the timer runs out.

Q4
Which atom pulls shared electrons towards itself the hardest?
Asodium
Bchlorine
Cfluorine
Diodine
Fluorine (electronegativity 4.0).
Core charge +7 like Cl and I, but only two shells: the smallest atom with the strongest pull.
Cambridge Worked example 1C–6Explain whether oxygen or nitrogen has the higher electronegativity.
1Define
Electronegativity is the ability of an atom to attract shared electrons to itself.
2Similarity
Both are in period 2, so both have two occupied shells.
3Difference
O (group 16) has core charge +6; N (group 15) has +5. So O has the smaller atomic radius.
4Relate back
O attracts electrons more strongly, so oxygen has the higher electronegativity.
Q5
Electronegativity: magnesium or strontium?
Mg. Both group 2 (core charge +2), but Mg has 3 shells and Sr has 5. Mg is smaller, so it attracts shared electrons more strongly.
Electronegativity: lithium or fluorine?
F. Both period 2, but F's core charge is +7 and Li's is +1. F is smaller and pulls harder.
Which has the higher first ionisation energy, sodium or chlorine? Why?
Chlorine. Both have three shells, but its core charge is +7 against +1, so it is smaller and holds its valence electrons more strongly.
Which atom is larger, magnesium or calcium? Why?
Calcium. Same core charge (+2), but one more shell.
Today we work on the ones not ticked yet.
Q1
Lithium, sodium and potassium are dropped into water. Which reacts most vigorously?
Alithium
Bsodium
Cpotassium
Dall the same
Potassium.
It has the most shells, so its one valence electron is furthest out and lost most easily.
Q2
Why is potassium a more reactive metal than sodium?
Same core charge (+1), but K has one more shell. Its valence electron is further out and held more weakly, so it is lost more easily.
Why is fluorine a more reactive non-metal than chlorine?
Same core charge (+7), but F has one fewer shell. It is smaller, so it gains an electron more easily.

Electrostatic force of attractionthe attraction between positively and negatively charged particles that are not directly in contact
Core chargethe electrostatic force of attraction between valence electrons and the nucleus. It is the number of protons minus the number of inner-shell electrons
Atomic radiusa measure of the size of an atom, from the centre of its nucleus to its valence shell
Electronegativitythe ability of an atom to attract electrons towards itself. Affected by core charge and atomic radius
Ionisation energythe energy required to remove an electron from a gaseous atom or ion
First ionisation energythe energy required to remove the first, or outermost, electron from a gaseous atom
Metallic characterthe ability of a metal to lose its valence electrons and display common metallic properties
Why is caesium a more reactive metal than sodium?
Same core charge (+1), but caesium has more shells. Its valence electron is further out, held more weakly and lost more easily.

Q1
Helium is the second most abundant element in the universe. Can it still be a critical element?
Ano, there is plenty of it
Byes, it is essential and its supply is at risk
Cno, it is unreactive
Donly if it is radioactive
Yes.
On Earth it is scarce: it escapes into space, and we cannot make it. Yet MRI machines depend on it.
Q2
Are the terms 'essential element' and 'critical element' the same?
No.
Essential: needed, e.g. for life or for a product.
Critical: essential AND its supply is vulnerable to disruption.
Q3
About 80% of mined phosphorus is lost before it reaches our food. Where does most of it go?
Ainto the air
Binto rivers and lakes in runoff
Cit decays away
Dit turns into other elements
Farm runoff and wastewater.
The extra phosphate feeds algae: eutrophication.
Q4
What happens to most of the phosphorus that is mined? State two ways to recover or save it.
Most is used in fertiliser, and much of it washes off farms into waterways.
Compost food scraps to return it to the soil. Use time-release fertilisers. Recover it from wastewater.

Q5
Which of these is NOT a rare-earth element?
Aneodymium
Beuropium
Cyttrium
Dlead
Lead: a post-transition metal.
Rare earths: the lanthanides, plus scandium and yttrium.
Q6
What are gallium and indium used for? Could they be critical?
Ga: semiconductors and fuel cells. In: touch screens.
Yes: new technology depends on them, and both come mainly as by-products of mining other metals.
Q7
How are metalloids like metals? How are they like non-metals?
Like metals: shiny (lustrous) solids that conduct electricity.
Like non-metals: brittle, and in reactions they tend to gain electrons.
Electronegativity and ionisation energy sit between the two.
Q8
Tin ore is mostly tin oxide, SnO₂. How is tin metal taken out of it?
Adissolve it in water
Bheat it with carbon
Cfreeze it
Dpull it out with a magnet
Smelting: heat it with carbon (coal).
The carbon takes the oxygen, leaving molten tin and slag.
Q9
Outline how tin is extracted from its ore.
1Mine the ore. Heat it to 500 to 600 °C to burn off any sulfur.
2Smelt: heat the concentrate with coal in a furnace. Crude tin and slag form.
3Re-heat the slag (10 to 25% tin) to recover more tin.
4Refine the crude tin by heat treatment or electrolysis.
Name one critical element, one use, and one reason its supply is at risk.
e.g. helium: cools MRI magnets; it escapes the atmosphere and cannot be made.
What is smelting?
Heating and melting an ore (with carbon) to extract a metal.
What is slag?
The by-product of smelting: silicon dioxide and metal oxides.

Q1
We recover 60% of the helium that is thrown away. But demand grows 2% every year. The supply
Anow lasts forever
Blasts longer, but still runs out
Cruns out faster
Ddoes not change at all
Recycling slows the loss.
Growing demand eats the gain. Run the model and see.
Q2
Which post-transition metal can be recycled the most, and where does Australia's recycled lead come from?
Lead: 100% recyclable with no loss of properties. About 90% of Australia's scrap lead comes from lead–acid car batteries.
How is helium recycled?
The helium vented from MRI machines is trapped and re-liquefied for re-use.
Q3
Give one environmental, one economic and one social reason to recover critical elements.
Environmental: less mining damage, pollution and landfill waste.
Economic: cheaper than new ore. Recycled lead uses 35 to 40% less energy.
Social: less land-use conflict, fairer access to resources, local jobs.
Chapter 1 review Q14 (4 marks): a model answerExplain why helium is a critical element, even though it is one of the most abundant elements in the universe.
1Define
A critical element is essential to a nation's economy or security, and its supply is vulnerable to disruption.
2Essential
Helium is used in cryogenics, e.g. to cool the superconducting magnets in MRI machines.
3Supply at risk
It comes only from natural gas and radioactive decay. It is so light it escapes the atmosphere, and we cannot make it.
4Relate back
So, though abundant in the universe, it is scarce on Earth, while demand keeps growing.

Critical elementa chemical element essential to economic or national security and vulnerable to disruption of supply
Cryogenicsthe production and effects of substances at very low temperatures
Eutrophicationa dense growth of plant life from high concentrations of nutrients in water, commonly due to runoff from land
Boiling pointthe temperature at which a liquid boils
Melting pointthe temperature at which a solid melts
Orea deposit in Earth's crust containing one or more valuable minerals, typically with a high concentration of a certain element
Smeltingthe process of heating and melting an ore to extract a metal
Slaga mixture of silicon dioxide and metal oxides left over as a by-product from smelting
Circular economyan economy that functions on a continuous cycle, with a focus on optimising the re-use of resources and materials
Give one environmental and one economic reason to recover critical elements.
Environmental: less mining damage and waste. Economic: cheaper and uses less energy than mining new ore.
Critical elements
Critical element: essential to a nation's
economy or security, AND its
supply is vulnerable to disruption.
e.g. He, P, rare earths, post-transition
metals, metalloids (Ge, As, Te)
Helium and phosphorus
He: from natural gas + radioactive decay.
Uses: cryogenics (MRI magnets).
Problem: escapes the atmosphere,
cannot be made. Demand ↑ 2%/yr.
Recycle: trap MRI vent gas, re-liquefy.
P: phosphate rock (most in Morocco).
Uses: fertiliser, DNA, bones.
~80% lost in runoff: eutrophication.
Save: compost, time-release
fertiliser, recover from wastewater.
Rare-earth elements
= lanthanides + Sc + Y
Uses: Nd magnets, Eu phosphors (lights),
Gd MRI, Er lasers, Yb optical fibre.
Spread thin, mined as compounds: hard
and costly to extract. Ores may hold
radioactive Th, U.
<1% of electronic devices recycled.
Post-transition metals, metalloids
Post-transition: Al, Ga, In, Sn, Pb, Bi
In touch screens, Ga semiconductors,
Pb batteries, Sn solder.
Often by-products of other mining.
Metalloids: B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te
look like metals, react like
non-metals. Si, Ge semiconductors.
Critical: Ge, As, Te.
Extraction: smelting tin
Ore: rock rich in a valuable mineral.
1 roast sulfide ores at 500–600 °C
to burn off the sulfur
2 smelt: heat with coal (carbon)
→ crude tin + slag
3 re-heat slag (10–25% Sn) for more tin
4 refine: heat treatment or electrolysis
Lesson 10 goal: to compare linear
and circular economies, and why we recover.
Recycling: linear or circular
Linear: take → make → use → dispose
Circular economy: a continuous cycle
that re-uses resources and materials.
Pb: 100% recyclable, 35–40% less energy
Al: ~75% ever made is still in use
Ge: recovered from optical fibre scrap
Recycling slows the loss, but growing
demand can still use up the supply.
Why recover elements?
Env: less mining damage, pollution, waste
Econ: cheaper, less energy, jobs
Social: fewer land-use conflicts, fair
access, less harm near mines
! Essential is not the same as critical.
Critical = essential + supply at risk.
